en: Then, having had the mandala ground smeared with fragrant substances mixed with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) consecrated with the mantra *oṃ āḥ hūṃ*, and having had it strewn with a profusion of beautiful flowers, at the time of afternoon—
having bathed, being pure, with limbs scented with fragrance and adorned with variegated ornaments;
Wearing white, unstained garments, he is likewise adorned with a turban.
Her body is purified by bathing, fragrant with clean perfumes, and adorned with various ornaments; she wears fresh white garments, and her crown is beautifully embellished.

According to this statement, he is adorned with ornaments such as necklaces, bracelets, anklets, armlets, earrings, rings, girdles, and finger-rings given by the donor; [he is consecrated] with the mantras *oṃ hūṃ svāhā* in their proper order.

Adorned with a crown and ornaments made of gold cloth and other materials over which *oṃ vajroṣṇīṣa hūṃ phaṭ* has been recited seven times, one should sit in the center of the maṇḍala ground facing east; alternatively, having sat in the eastern part of the maṇḍala facing west, possessing the yoga of the Lord of the Mandala (*cakreśa*), one should prepare maṇḍalas with sandalwood and other substances at the locations of the deities, visualize the respective pledge-mandala (*samayacakra*) therein, cause the wisdom-mandala (*jñānamaṇḍala*) to enter—drawn by the light from the seed-syllable in the heart—and perform the worship, praise, and tasting of nectar as far as required.
Outside the consecrated maṇḍala, one should consecrate the vases situated in the eastern and other directions; alternatively, facing north, one may consecrate those located in the northeast corner.

Having adorned them with ornaments such as necklaces, anklets, armlets, bracelets, waist-bands, and rings offered by the patron—according to the words [of the scripture]—one should, in the proper sequence, recite: *oṃ āḥ hūṃ svāhā* and *oṃ vajra auṣṇīṣa hūṃ phaṭ*.

Having adorned golden head-ornaments—which have been recited seven times—with garments and so forth, one should sit in the center of the mandala ground facing east, or else sit facing the east or west of the mandala.

One endowed with the yoga of the Lord of the Wheel should construct a maṇḍala of candana and so forth in the abode of the deities. Having clearly visualized the samaya-maṇḍala accordingly, one should cause the wisdom-maṇḍala—invited there by the light rays from the seed-syllable at the heart—to enter, and perform as many offerings, praises, and partakings of nectar as possible.
Outside the visualized maṇḍala, one should place the vases situated in the directions such as the east, or in other directions, those located in the northeast (īśāna) corner facing north.
In that regard, their characteristics are stated according to the distinctions of pacifying rites (*śāntika*) and so forth.

Likewise, for the jar used in rites of pacification (*śānti*) and nourishment (*puṣṭi*), the interior of the belly is sixteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in circumference. From the bottom of the belly to the edge of the rim, it is twenty finger-breadths in length. The two hanging lips are two finger-breadths each. The neck is six finger-breadths. The mouth, from one lip-edge to the other, is eight finger-breadths. The opening of the mouth consists of two parts of those eight finger-breadths. The width of the two lips is by the lower portion.

Furthermore, for both the pacifying and enriching [rites], the circumference of the belly of the vase is sixteen finger-widths (aṅgula). From the bottom of the belly to the opening and the spout, the height is twenty finger-widths. The measure of the downward-turning spout is two finger-widths. The neck is six finger-widths. The opening, from one end of the spout to the other, is eight finger-widths.
Two parts of the eightfold division are the opening of the mouth; one part is the width of the two lips.

Regarding the *ghaṭa* (vase) for the rites of causing enmity (*vidveṣaṇa*) and expulsion (*uccāṭana*): the circumference of its belly is twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), and its height is twenty-four finger-breadths. The neck is eight finger-breadths long and curved; the mouth is six finger-breadths wide; and the two lips are one finger-breadth each.
Just as a potter fashions a jar for the purposes of subduing or attracting.
The vases for the empowerments and the summoning are to be fashioned by the artisan exactly as prescribed.

For the rite of paralyzing (stambhana), the pestle should be short, measuring sixteen finger-breadths in circumference and height; its neck is four finger-breadths [in width], its mouth is six finger-breadths [in diameter], and it has thick lips of two finger-breadths.

The vase of restraint is short, being sixteen finger-widths (*aṅgula*) in circumference and height; the neck is four finger-widths; the mouth is six finger-widths; and the spout is thick and two finger-widths.
For all rites, such as those for pacification and so forth, the vessels prescribed therein should be taken.
Regarding the all-purpose [vase], one should take up those vases mentioned for rites such as pacification and so forth.

Even though other tantras state, "Black roots, protruding lips, long necks, and large bellies," one should understand that [the measurements] such as sixteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) and so forth also apply here.
% "Black roots and protruding lips, long necks and large bellies"—as taught in other tantras, this should be understood to refer to those [measures] of sixteen finger-breadths and so on.
Therefore, that which possesses the aforementioned characteristics is described as follows:
it may be made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay.
And the practitioner, observing the vow, should place the flask as it was obtained within the mandala.
A vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay—whichever is available—the one who observes the ascetic vows should arrange upon the mandala.
One should cast coral, silver, gold, ruby, and pearl— these five auspicious gems— into the interior of the jar.
One should place within the belly of the vases those possessing the five jewels—cat's-eye, gold, silver, ruby, and pearl.
Likewise, one should place within the belly of the vase the five grains, which are highly praised: barley, wheat, beans, sesame, and rice.
Rice, wheat, mung beans, sesame seeds, and likewise pulses—those taught as grains should be placed within the belly of the jar.
One should cast in the roots of these five medicinal herbs: bṛhatī, kaṇṭakārī, sahadevā, aparājitā, and daṇḍotpalā.
These are glossed in Newari:
*brīhati*, *kaṇḍakārī*, *hasadevāparājita*, and the root of *daṇḍotpala*; these five medicinal substances should also be included.
One should take five sprouts— of the mango, the udumbara, the aśoka, the aśvattha, and likewise the nāgaja— to adorn the mouths of the jars.
By offering *āmra*, *udumbara*, *aśoka*, *aśvattha*, and likewise *nāgakesara*—these five types of branches—the mouth of the vase should be adorned.
One should wrap the neck of the jar with a large white cloth;
upon the cloth, the one skilled in the ritual should place a very white thread.
The necks of the vases should be bound with a great white cloth; the one skilled in the ritual should arrange five cords upon the cloth.
The wise one should draw the seed-syllable or the emblem of all the maṇḍala deities on the side of the jar, having prepared it with sandalwood and other substances.

For all those belonging to the mandala, the wise one should draw either the seed-syllables or the hand-symbols upon the surface of the flask, having prepared them with sandalwood and other substances.

The wise practitioner should place these [vessels], filled with water and endowed with jewels and other [substances], consecrated by their own mantra, in a number equal to that of the deities and the enemies.

In this context, those possessing jewels and so forth are highly praised according to their respective tantras. One who possesses water and is endowed with intelligence should arrange the divine cooling substances.

In this manner, one should place such vases—each individually arranged in the shape of a mandala upon the surface of a canopy according to the sequence for depositing the signs of the *rajo-maṇḍala* to be described later—either seated upon appropriate seats atop a mandala of fragrant substances and so forth, or arranged in rows. Having placed them before oneself with their necks wrapped in white threads over which the mantra "Oṃ vajraśikhara ruṭ maṭ diśāṃ baddha 2 hūṃ phaṭ" has been recited seven times, one should first contemplate emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and subsequently visualize them as being made of jewels by means of the syllable *vaṃ*. In the absence of the five aforementioned jewels, other suitable materials may be inserted.

Thus, such vases as these are to be arranged individually one by one upon a mandala of fragrant substances and the like—which will be explained below under the section on the placement of the ritual marks (*cihna*) upon the colored powder mandala—either in the form of a mandala or in rows, upon seats appropriate to each.

Reciting "oṃ vajra śikhara ruru tāṃ tāṃ diśaṃ bandha hūṃ" seven times, one should wrap a white cord or similar material around the neck and place it in front; then, having first visualized it as emptiness, one should finally meditate upon it as being of the nature of jewels, arising from the syllable BAṂ.
If the five jewels as they have been described are not available, other jewels should be introduced.
In some places, mung beans are prescribed for the storage of grain.
Furthermore, in the absence of the five sprouts, the Blessed One has authorized the ritual even with a single sprout from the Bodhi tree.
The Blessed One has said: "If the five branches are absent, those who understand the ritual may [proceed] even with a single branch of the Bodhi tree."
If the aforementioned medicinal herbs are unavailable,
other medicinal herbs should be substituted.
If one desires the acquisition of wealth through agriculture, the Vijaya and Sārvakarmika yantras, containing jewels within them, should be prepared.
If resources are meager, one should use precious gems for the Vijaya and Sarvakarmika [vases].
In that case as well,
the victory vase must necessarily be made with a jewel at its core.

In the victory vase (*vijayakalaśa*), however, one should write the emblem or seed-syllable (*bīja*) of the Lord—situated upon a universal lotus (*viśvājja*) in the center of the source of phenomena (*dharmodayā*), and appropriately on either the moon or the sun—in the other vases, one should write the respective emblems or seed-syllables of the deities, situated upon universal lotuses on either the moon or the sun.

In the case of the *vijaya* (victory) vase, one should draw the master’s emblem or seed-syllable as appropriate upon a moon or sun disk resting on a multicolored lotus in the center of the source of phenomena (*dharmodayā*). In the other vases, one should likewise draw their respective emblems or seed-syllables upon a moon or sun disk resting on a multicolored lotus, according to the nature of each deity.
In whichever maṇḍala there are as many deities, there are that many vases for them.

Alternatively, [the vases] are for those situated within the womb-chambers (*garbhapuṭa*). In that case, there are four for the Family Mothers (*kulamātṛ*) and five for the Tathāgatas; or else, there are five for the Tathāgatas alone. Or again, there is one for the Lord (*adhipati*), one for the four Tathāgatas, one for the four Family Mothers, one for the six [deities] beginning with Rūpavajrā, and one for the quartet of Wrathful Deities (*krodha*)—thus making five. Alternatively, there is only one for the Leader (*nāyaka*) himself. In these various positions, an additional "all-purpose" (*sārvakārmika*) vase must be prepared for the purpose of sprinkling the disciples and others.

Some do not accept this; rather, they hold that even in the absence of a second jar, the leader’s insignia should be drawn on the *vijaya* jar, and on its left, the insignia for all rites (*sārvakarmika*)—this is another position. That insignia belongs to Vighnāntaka.

Alternatively, they reside solely within the heart of the palace. Among them, there are four for the Mothers of the Families (*kula-mātṛ*) and five for the Tathāgatas. Or else, there are five exclusively for the Tathāgatas. Alternatively, there is one for the Lord (*adhipati*), one for the four Tathāgatas, one for the four Mothers of the Families, and one for the six [deities] beginning with Vajrarūpā.

This is one of the four wrathful deities, making five [in total]. Alternatively, it may belong to the principal deity alone. In these directions, the *sarvakarmika* (all-purpose) vase should be offered as a supplementary offering for the purpose of purifying the disciples and others. Some do not accept this, and if even two vases are not available, [the procedure continues accordingly].

Regarding the instruction that "one should draw the symbol of the *sarvakarmika* [vase] on the left side of the primary mark on the *vijaya* vase," this refers to another perspective; its symbol is that of Vighnantaka.

According to the position that the four symbols of Vairocana and the others should also be drawn in the four directions, the symbol of the central leader is placed above the symbol of Vairocana; it is stated in some sources that it should be situated right there, upon the upper lip. There is also another position that [the symbols] of Locanā and the others should likewise be in the four intermediate directions.

Regarding the statement that "the four symbols of Vairocana and the others should also be drawn in the four directions," according to one interpretation, they are placed above the symbol of the principal deity, Vairocana. According to some, it is explained that they are situated right there, above the lips. Furthermore, the phrase "those of Locanā and the others are likewise in the intermediate directions" refers to another position.
Alternatively,
there are separate jars for the five Buddhas, the four goddesses, and the four wrathful deities;
each is adorned with earrings and bears the sixfold symbols, such as the vajra and so forth.
Thus, there are fifteen.

Alternatively, as it is said: "The five Buddhas and the four goddesses, the vases of the four wrathful deities, each with its own single swirl, and the six such as Rūpavajrā—these possess the [respective] signs; thus, there are fifteen."

A different position than those stated has been proposed by someone else, which is inconsistent. Thus, in the Mañjuvajra-maṇḍala, the arrangement of the number of vases is twenty, ten, six, two, one, and fifteen.

Those other positions mentioned apart from the positions already described are not logical. Thus, regarding Mañjuvajra, the number of vases is established as twenty, ten, six, two, one, and fifteen; this is the classification of the vases for the mandala.

In the Piṇḍīkrama maṇḍala, however, according to the second fivefold system, the distinction is as follows: there is one [mandala] for the Tathāgatas, one for the Mothers, one for Caturūpavajrā and the others, one for the eight Bodhisattvas, and one for the ten Wrathful Deities.

Regarding the two groups of five in the mandala of the *Saṃpuṭatantra*, the distinction is as follows: one for the Tathāgatas, one for the Mothers, one for the four such as Vajrarūpā, one for the eight Bodhisattvas, and one for the ten Wrathful Deities.
Alternatively:

one for each of the two sons of one's own direction, six for the wrathful ones, and likewise for the women; and separately, one for the obstacle-removers, the enemies, and the gate-guardians—thus there are twenty.
Some say:

"Alternatively, one [deity] belongs to each of the two sons of one's own side, as well as to the six wrathful ones and their consorts; furthermore, there are twenty for each of the heart[-mantras], the gatekeepers, and the obstructors and enemies. This is the view of some.

In the Vajrasattva maṇḍala described in the *Sampuṭa*, according to the second fivefold system, there is one [vase] for those situated in the inner enclosure (*garbhapuṭa*), one for those in the second enclosure, one for the eight goddesses of the cardinal directions, one for the eight goddesses of the intermediate directions, and one for the gatekeepers; this is the distinction. Alternatively, there are separate vases for the Tathāgata family, the Mothers, and the Gatekeepers. In the second enclosure, there is one for the goddesses of the cardinal directions and one for the goddesses of the intermediate directions. In the third enclosure, there is one for those situated on the left in the cardinal directions and one for those situated on the right.
"One for those situated in the corners, one outside of them for those situated in the corners, and one for all-purpose rites; thus, some say there are twenty."

Regarding the fifth [chapter] of the second section as taught in the *Vajradhātumaṇḍala* of the *Saṃpuṭa*: the distinction is that there is one for those residing in the heart of the palace, one for those residing in the second palace, one for the goddesses of the eight directions, one for the goddesses of the corners, and one for the gatekeepers.

Alternatively, there shall be one vase each for the Tathāgatas, the Mothers of the Families, and the Gatekeepers; one for the goddesses of the directions in the second tier; one for the goddesses of the intermediate directions; one for those situated on the left in the third tier; and one for those situated on the right.
"One for those situated at the corners, one for those situated outside of them, and one for the *sarvakarmika* [monk]; thus there are twenty"—this is the view of some.

In the Saṃvara maṇḍala, there are five [deities] for each of the five wheels (*cakras*), making five. Alternatively, there are only five for those situated in the central enclosure (*garbhapuṭa*). Or again, there are four for each of these four wheels, making nine; or alternatively, there are thirteen for those situated in the central enclosure and the Samaya wheel. In the mind wheel (*cittacakra*), there is one for the cardinal directions and one for the intermediate directions; likewise in the speech wheel (*vākcakra*) and the body wheel (*kāyacaktra*), making nineteen. In these systems, when performing the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) for each deity, an additional *Sārvakarmika* Khaṇḍarohā should be installed.

In the mandala of glorious Cakrasaṃvara, there are five [deities], one for each of the five wheels. Alternatively, there are five who reside solely within the heart palace. Alternatively, there are nine: the five forms of these [deities] and the four from the four wheels. Alternatively, there are thirteen: the one residing in the central palace and those residing in the samaya wheel.

There is one for those situated in the cardinal directions of the mind wheel (*cittacakra*) and one for those situated in the intermediate directions. Likewise, there are nineteen [deities] for the speech wheel (*vākcakra*) and the body wheel (*kāyacakra*). In these directions, as for the placement of each respective deity, the all-accomplishing *Karmasarvārthasādhikā* (Umā) should be placed in excess.
Following this principle, the number of vases for other mandalas should also be understood according to what is appropriate.

Therein, due to its preeminence and the abundance of ritual duties, one should place upon the *vijaya-ghaṭa* (victory-pitcher) either a conch or a lotus vessel containing the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) as obtained, mixed with fragrant water, consecrated by the mantra *HŪṂ*, and rendered into the nectar of gnosis (*jñānāmṛta*) by reciting seven times the three principles (*tritattva*)—namely, *OṂ VAJRĀMṚTODAKA ṬHA ṬHA HŪṂ*—along with a vajra bound with a garland of flowers.

In the center, reciting "Oṃ tapte mahātapte svāhā," one should instantly visualize the circle of deities with their seats within the water that has the nature of the drawn-in waters of the Mandākinī. Then, having summoned the wisdom-circle (*jñānacakra*) by means of rays from the seed-syllable in one's own heart, one should offer water for the feet, water for rinsing the mouth, and the guest-offering (*argha*). One should then contemplate that circle as entering the pledge-circle (*samayacakra*), melting through great passion, and becoming of one flavor with the previously placed water in the form of bodhicitta. Likewise, one should contemplate the pledge-deity within the emblem as being unified with the wisdom-deity.

Because it is the principal [substance] and because there is much activity to be performed, one should consecrate the contents of the *vijaya-kalaśa* (victory vase) seven times with the mantra "Oṃ vajrāmṛtodbhava hūṃ" and also with the three syllables, thereby transforming them into the nectar of primordial wisdom (*jñānāmṛta*). These consist of the nature of vajra-atomic particles (*vajra-paramāṇu*) along with whatever five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) have been obtained.

Having consecrated [the vessel] with *hūṃ* containing fragrant water, place within it a vajra whose handle is bound with a garland of flowers upon a lotus bud, and recite: *oṃ tatpate mahātapte svāhā*.

Having thus summoned [the deities], one should visualize in an instant the divine wheel together with its seats arising from the nature of the aforementioned divine water. Then, before the nectar of primordial wisdom (*jñānāmṛta*) invited by the seed-syllable at one’s own heart, one should offer the water for the feet, the water for the face, and the offering water (*arghya*). Thereafter, they are caused to enter the commitment wheel (*samayacakra*).

Meditate that, having been melted by great passion, it becomes of one taste with the water previously poured in and the nature of the bodhicitta. Furthermore, contemplate that the sign (nimitta) becomes one with the wisdom deity (jñānadeva) of the commitment deity (samayadeva).

Then, having grasped [the water] with the left fist up to the end of the flower garland attached to the vajra while reciting the *hūṃ* mantra, one should consecrate the water either one hundred and eight times with the heart-mantra of the Lord of the Mandala (*cakreśa*), or by means of the mantra *oṃ vajrodaka hūṃ*. Into that [water], one should cast three white flowers consecrated with the *kuṇḍali* mantra.

Furthermore, whichever flask belongs to a particular deity, that [flask] should be consecrated one hundred and eight times, or twenty-one times, or seven times with that deity’s mantra; having grasped it up to the end of the flower garland attached to the vajra above, one should likewise cast a flower into it.

Then, having grasped the edge of the vajra with the left fist and consecrated it with *hūṃ*, one should consecrate the water with the essence-mantra of the Lord of the Mandala (*cakreśvara*) one hundred and eight times, or with *oṃ vajra udaka hūṃ*. Having thus consecrated it, one should place three white flowers that have been consecrated by swirling [the water] therein.

Furthermore, whichever deity a particular flask belongs to, one should consecrate it with its mantra one hundred and eight, twenty-one, or seven times, holding it at the end of a garland of vajra-flowers. Likewise, flowers should also be inserted [into the flask].

Thereafter, having worshipped the victory-pitchers (vijaya-kalaśa) and the others with flowers and other offerings, and having sprinkled them with water for all rites (sārvakarmika-vāri) using their very sprouts for the sake of protection, one should say, "Until the completion of the mandala activities here, you shall ward off obstacles," and after giving the bali offering and performing the ritual sipping of water (upaspṛśya), one should ring the bell while preceded by the praise beginning with "Akṣobhyavajra."

Then, having properly worshipped the *victory* (*vijaya*) and other vases with flowers and so forth, one should purify them with water from the *all-purpose* (*sarvakarmika*) vessel using its sprouts for the sake of protection, saying: "For as long as the activities of the mandala are not completed, please ward off all obstructors! Having offered the *bali* and touched [the vase], [one should proceed].
One should ring the bell preceded by a praise beginning with "Akṣobhyavajra" and so forth.

Having drawn a little water from each of those jars, one should place it in a conch shell or similar vessel situated on a mechanical device at the northern side of the eastern door of the maṇḍala house, for the purpose of sprinkling oneself and the disciples. Alternatively, another [teacher] says that one should set aside a single "all-purpose jar" (sārvakarmika-kalaśa), provided with a bundle of *kuśa* grass, measuring one span (*vitasti*) in length, for that same purpose. One should perform the consecration, worship, and other rites for the jars three times daily or once daily.

Taking a small amount of water from each of those vases, one should place it in the conch-shell vessel (dung-chos) and so forth situated in the northern part of the eastern entrance of the mandala house, for the purpose of performing the purification sprinkling (bsang-gtor) for oneself and the disciples.

Regarding the statement, "The *sarvakarmika* flask itself, provided with a bundle of *kuśa* grass, should be placed there for that purpose," this is from another source. As for the praises, offerings, and so forth directed toward the flasks, they should be performed three times or once each day.
The mantras of the Wheel Lord (Cakreśa) and others, however,
should be sought in the respective *sādhanas* and other texts for each maṇḍala.

Furthermore, the concise version will be explained here again at the time of describing the forms, colors, insignia, and so forth of the deities of the maṇḍala that are to be discussed. (Note: This is a rewriting of the *Niṣpannayogāvalī*! The concise version will be explained once more in this very work, at the time of stating the forms, colors, and symbols of the deities of the maṇḍala.

Here, for the purpose of employing it in the rites of the mandala and so forth, one should first place either the *vijaya-kalaśa* or the *sārvakarmika-kalaśa* upon the pericarp of an eight-petaled lotus drawn with white powder or other colors. Then, according to the procedure to be described, one should place the five-colored thread (*pañcaraṅgika-sūtra*) that has been consecrated (*adhivāsita*) in the eastern petal; the vajra in a vessel of gold or similar material in the southern petal; the bell in the northern petal; and the containers for the five powders (*pañca-rajas*) in the corner petals as appropriate. With water from that flask, while reciting the *kuṇḍalī-mantra*, one should sprinkle the powder and the thread.

For the purpose of the activities such as the mandala, one should first draw an eight-petaled lotus with white colored powder or the like; in its center, one should place either a *vijaya* vase or a *sarvakarmika* vase.

On the eastern petal, the five-colored marking threads, which have been consecrated through the ritual that will be explained, are placed in a vessel made of gold or similar materials. On the south is a vajra; on the north, a vajra bell. On the western and corner petals, the vessels for the five colored powders are placed as appropriate.
Having recited the mantra while circling [the vessel], one should perform the purification (saṃtarpaṇa) of the colored powders and the marking threads with the water from the vase.
Thus concludes the procedure for the consecration of the vase (kalaśādhivāsanavidhi).
Thus concludes the ritual for the consecration of the vase (*kalaśa-adhiṣṭhāna-vidhi*).
